hello.title: Hello, D
hello.summary: Write your first D program: import std.stdio, start in main and print text and numbers with writeln and write.
hello.lesson.0: A D program is a text file that ends in `.d`. A compiler such as `dmd` or `ldc2` turns it into a program that you can run. Here is the classic first program. It prints one line of text.
hello.lesson.2: Let us read it line by line. `import std.stdio;` loads the module for input and output (`stdio` means standard input and output) from Phobos, the standard library of D. `void main()` is the function where every program starts. `void` means that it gives back no value. The braces `{` and `}` hold the code of the function.
hello.lesson.3: `writeln` writes text to the screen and then ends the line. Text in double quotes, like `"Hello, world!"`, is called a **string**. Every statement ends with a semicolon `;`.
hello.lesson.5: You can give `writeln` several values, separated by commas. It prints them one after another, **without** spaces between them. Numbers need no quotes, and D calculates `2 + 3` before it prints. Text in quotes is printed exactly as it is.
hello.lesson.7: `write` prints like `writeln`, but it does not end the line. The next output continues on the same line. `writeln()` with nothing inside only ends the line.
hello.lesson.9: A **comment** starts with `//` and goes to the end of the line. The compiler ignores it. In this course, comments only show results. `*` multiplies and `-` subtracts.
hello.lesson.11: Inside a string, `\n` starts a new line and `\"` prints a double quote. These pairs are called escape sequences.
hello.lesson.13: D is case-sensitive: `writeln` works, but `Writeln` or `WRITELN` is an error. A missing semicolon is also an error, and the compiler tells you the line.
hello.card.1: `void main() { }` is where the program starts
hello.card.4: `// comment` is ignored, `;` ends a statement
hello-1.explain: `writeln` comes from `std.stdio`. `print` and `echo` do not exist in D, and `System.out.println` is Java.
hello-2.explain: D calculates `4 + 5` first and prints the result `9` right after the text.
hello-3.explain: `write` does not end the line, so `A`, `B` and `C` appear on the same line.
hello-4.explain: `writeln` prints its values one after another without spaces. It does not add them.
hello-5.statement: Every D program starts running in the function `main`.
hello-5.explain: `void main()` is the starting point. A program without `main` cannot be built.
hello-6.prompt: Complete the code so that it prints `Hi` and `there` on two lines.
hello-6.explain: `writeln` ends the line after `Hi`. With `write`, both words would be on one line.
hello-7.prompt: Complete the import so that `writeln` works.
hello-7.explain: `writeln` lives in the module `std.stdio` of the standard library.
hello-8.explain: The text and the number are separated by a comma. `+` cannot join a string and a number.
hello-9.prompt: Put the lines in order so that the program prints `Start` and then `1 2 3`.
hello-9.explain: `Start` comes first and ends its line. The two `write` calls and the last `writeln` build the second line.
hello-10.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
hello-10.pairs.2: loads the input and output module
hello-12.explain: D is case-sensitive. The function is `writeln` with a small `w`: `writeln("Bye");`.
variables.title: Variables and types
variables.summary: Store values in variables with the types int, double, string and bool, and let auto and immutable help you.
variables.lesson.0: A **variable** is a name for a value. In D you write the type first, then the name, then `=` and the value. `int` holds whole numbers, `double` holds decimal numbers, `string` holds text and `bool` holds `true` or `false`.
variables.lesson.2: You give a variable a new value with `=`. `score += 2` is short for `score = score + 2`. `-=`, `*=` and `/=` work the same way. The type of a variable never changes: putting a string into an `int` variable is an error.
variables.lesson.4: D calculates with `+`, `-`, `*` and `/`, and `*` and `/` come before `+` and `-`. When you divide two `int` values, the result is an `int` and the rest is dropped. `%` gives the rest of a division. If one of the numbers is a `double`, like `7.0`, the result is a `double`.
variables.lesson.7: With `auto` instead of a type, the compiler picks the type from the value. `typeof(x).stringof` gives the name of the type of `x` as text, so you can check it.
variables.lesson.9: A variable marked `immutable` can never change after it gets its value. Use it for values that must stay fixed. Like `auto`, `immutable` can pick the type by itself: `immutable weeks = 3;` is an `int`.
variables.lesson.11: If you try to change an `immutable` variable, for example with `days = 8;`, the program does not compile.
variables.lesson.12: A variable without a value gets a default value: `0` for `int`, `false` for `bool` and an empty text for `string`. A `double` starts as `nan`, which means "not a number". It reminds you that you forgot to set a value.
variables.card.2: `auto x = 3.5;` the compiler picks the type
variables-1.explain: `b` gets `10` when it is created. Changing `a` later does not change `b`, so `1 + 10` is `11`.
variables-2.explain: 17 divided by 5 is 3 with a rest of 2. With two `int` values, `/` gives `3` and `%` gives `2`.
variables-3.prompt: Which line creates a variable that can never change?
variables-3.explain: `immutable` values are fixed. `auto` and `int` variables can change, and `var` is not a D keyword.
variables-4.explain: `2.5` has a decimal point, so `auto` makes `x` a `double`.
variables-5.explain: `n` is an `int`. A variable keeps its type, so it cannot hold the string `"five"`.
variables-6.explain: A `bool` without a value starts as `false`.
variables-7.prompt: Complete the code so that it prints `3.5`.
variables-7.explain: With `7.0` the division uses decimal numbers. `7 / 2` would give `3`, and a string cannot be divided.
variables-8.prompt: Complete the code so that it prints `Ben`.
variables-8.explain: Text in double quotes is a `string`. It does not fit into `int`, `bool` or `char`.
variables-9.prompt: Build a line that creates a `double` variable `price` with the value 2.5.
variables-9.explain: Type, name, `=`, value and a semicolon. An `int` cannot hold `2.5`.
variables-10.prompt: Put the lines in order so that the program prints `12`.
variables-10.explain: `x` becomes `3 * 2 = 6`, then `6 + 6 = 12`. Adding first would give `(3 + 6) * 2 = 18`.
variables-11.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
variables-12.explain: `apples * price` is a `double` (1.5), which does not fit into an `int`. Write `double total = apples * price;`.
strings.title: Strings
strings.summary: Join strings with ~, read characters and slices, use std.string functions and format output with writefln.
strings.lesson.0: In D you join two strings with `~` (the tilde), not with `+`. `s ~= "!"` adds text to the end of `s`.
strings.lesson.2: `s.length` gives the number of characters. `s[0]` is the first character, because counting starts at `0`. `s[1 .. 4]` is a **slice**: the characters from position 1 up to, but not including, position 4. Inside the brackets, `$` means the length, so `s[$ - 1]` is the last character.
strings.lesson.5: The module `std.string` has many useful functions. `strip` removes spaces at the start and the end, `toUpper` and `toLower` change the case, `indexOf` gives the position of a text (or `-1` if it is not there) and `replace` swaps one text for another. You call them with a dot after the string: `s.toUpper()`.
strings.lesson.7: `"a" + "b"` does not compile, because `+` is only for numbers. `~` only joins strings, so `"Age: " ~ age` with an `int` variable `age` does not compile either.
strings.lesson.9: To turn a number into a string, use `to!string(n)` from the module `std.conv`. `to!int("42")` goes the other way. The `!` gives `to` the type you want to get.
strings.lesson.12: `writefln` prints a format string and ends the line. Each placeholder is replaced by the next value: `%s` fits any value, `%d` a whole number and `%.2f` a decimal number with two digits after the point. `format` from `std.string` works the same way but gives back the string instead of printing it.
strings-1.explain: `~` joins the two strings without adding a space.
strings-2.explain: `banana` has 6 characters, and `s[1]` is the second one, `a`. `writeln` prints both without a space.
strings-3.explain: Positions 3, 4 and 5 are `b`, `o` and `a`. The end position 6 is not included.
strings-4.explain: `+` does not work on strings. Use `~` together with `to!string(10)`, or `writeln("Score: ", 10)`.
strings-5.explain: Counting starts at 0: `H` is 0, `e` is 1, and the first `l` is at position 2.
strings-6.statement: This code prints the last character, `t`.
strings-6.explain: `$` is the length of the string, so `s[$ - 1]` is the last character.
strings-7.prompt: Complete the code so that it prints `Hi, Ana`.
strings-7.explain: In D, `~` joins strings. `+`, `&` and `*` do not work with strings.
strings-8.prompt: Complete the code so that it prints `D IS FUN`.
strings-8.explain: `toUpper` from `std.string` turns all letters into capital letters.
strings-9.prompt: Build the line that prints `price` with two digits after the decimal point.
strings-9.explain: `writefln` reads the format string. `%.2f` prints a decimal number with two digits; `%d` is only for whole numbers.
strings-10.prompt: Put the lines in order so that the program prints `Hello, World!`.
strings-10.explain: First create `s`, then add `, ` and `World!` in this order, and print at the end.
strings-11.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
strings-11.pairs.2: removes spaces at the start and end
strings-11.pairs.4: turns text into a whole number
strings-12.explain: `~` cannot join a string and an `int`. Convert the number first: `"Age: " ~ to!string(age)`.
conditions.title: Decisions
conditions.summary: Let your program choose with if, else, the ?: operator and switch.
conditions.lesson.0: `if` runs code only when a condition is `true`. The condition goes in parentheses `( )`, the code in braces. `else if` checks another condition, and `else` runs when no condition was `true`. You compare values with `==` (equal), `!=` (not equal), `<`, `>`, `<=` and `>=`.
conditions.lesson.2: You combine conditions with `&&` (and: both must be `true`), `||` (or: at least one must be `true`) and `!` (not: turns `true` into `false` and back).
conditions.lesson.4: The operator `? :` picks one of two values: `cond ? a : b` gives `a` when `cond` is `true` and `b` otherwise. Here `n % 2 == 0` checks if `n` is even.
conditions.lesson.6: `=` gives a value, `==` compares. If you write `if (x = 5)` by mistake, D stops with an error instead of running wrong code.
conditions.lesson.8: `switch` compares one value with several `case` labels and runs the matching one. A case can list several values, separated by commas. Each case ends with `break`. D does not let a case run into the next one: forgetting `break` is an error. `default` runs when no case matches, and D requires it.
conditions.lesson.12: `case 80: .. case 89:` matches every value from 80 to 89, both ends included.
conditions-1.explain: 15 is not at least 20, but it is at least 10, so the `else if` branch runs.
conditions-2.explain: `a > 5` is `false`, but `b > 5` is `true`. With `||` one `true` side is enough.
conditions-3.explain: `3` is listed in `case 2, 3:`, so that case runs and `break` ends the `switch`.
conditions-4.explain: The first case has no `break`, so it would run into the next case. D does not allow this and stops with an error.
conditions-5.explain: `x = 4` is an assignment, not a comparison. D does not accept it as a condition. Write `x == 4`.
conditions-7.prompt: Complete the code so that it prints `negative`.
conditions-7.explain: `-3 < 0` is `true`, so `? :` picks the first value, `negative`.
conditions-8.prompt: Complete the code so that it prints `other`.
conditions-8.explain: `default` runs when no `case` matches. `XL` is not `S`.
conditions-9.prompt: Build the first line of an `if` that checks that `age` is at least 18 and `member` is `true`.
conditions-9.explain: The condition goes in parentheses. `&&` means and; D has no `and` keyword. `>=` means at least.
conditions-10.prompt: Put the lines in order so that the program prints `Warm`.
conditions-10.explain: `22 > 25` is `false`, so the `else` branch runs. It must contain the line that prints `Warm`.
conditions-11.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
conditions-11.pairs.1: at least one must be true
conditions-11.pairs.3: checks if two values are equal
conditions-12.explain: The condition needs parentheses: `} else if (score >= 50) {`.
loops.title: Loops
loops.summary: Repeat code with for, foreach over ranges like 0 .. 5, while and do-while, and control loops with break and continue.
loops.lesson.0: A `for` loop has three parts in its parentheses, separated by semicolons: a start (`int i = 1`), a condition that is checked before each round (`i <= 3`) and a step that runs after each round. `i++` adds 1 to `i`, and `i--` subtracts 1.
loops.lesson.3: `foreach (i; 0 .. 3)` is the easiest way to count. `0 .. 3` is a **range**: the numbers from 0 up to 3, **without** 3. The loop runs once for each number, and `i` holds the current one.
loops.lesson.5: `foreach` also walks over the characters of a string, one after another. `foreach_reverse` walks backwards.
loops.lesson.8: `while` repeats its code as long as the condition is `true`. Make sure something inside the loop changes, or the loop never ends.
loops.lesson.10: `do { } while (cond);` checks the condition **after** each round, so the code runs at least once.
loops.lesson.12: `continue` jumps straight to the next round, and `break` ends the loop at once.
loops.card.4: `break` ends the loop, `continue` goes to the next round
loops-1.explain: `1 .. 5` gives 1, 2, 3 and 4 (5 is not included). 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 is 10.
loops-3.prompt: How many lines does this print?
loops-3.explain: `2 .. 6` gives 2, 3, 4 and 5. The end, 6, is not included.
loops-4.explain: When `i` is 3, `break` ends the loop before `write(i)`, so only 0, 1 and 2 are printed.
loops-5.explain: `0 .. 3` gives 0, 1 and 2, so the code runs 3 times.
loops-6.explain: A `do`-`while` loop runs once before it checks the condition. `6 < 3` is `false`, so it stops after one round.
loops-7.prompt: Complete the loop so that it prints 0, 1 and 2.
loops-7.explain: A range is written with two dots: `0 .. 3`.
loops-8.prompt: Complete the loop so that it prints 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1.
loops-8.explain: The loop runs while `n > 0`. With `>=` it would also print 0.
loops-9.prompt: Build the first line of a loop that repeats as long as `count` is smaller than 10.
loops-9.explain: `while` checks its condition before each round. `until` is not a D keyword.
loops-10.prompt: Put the lines in order so that the program prints `15`.
loops-10.explain: Create `total`, add 1 to 5 in the loop, and print once after the loop: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 is 15.
loops-11.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
loops-12.explain: The three parts of a `for` loop are separated by semicolons: `for (int i = 1; i <= 4; i++) {`.
functions.title: Functions
functions.summary: Write your own functions with parameters and return values, change variables with ref and chain calls with UFCS.
functions.lesson.0: A **function** is a named block of code that you can call again and again. You write the return type, the name and the parameters in parentheses, each with its type. `return` gives a value back to the caller. A `void` function gives nothing back. Functions are written outside of `main`.
functions.lesson.2: In D, a function can come before or after `main`. A parameter can have a default value with `=`. If you leave it out in the call, the default is used.
functions.lesson.4: A function can have several `return` statements. The first one that runs ends the function at once.
functions.lesson.6: If the return type is not `void`, every way through the function must end with `return` and a value. Otherwise the program does not compile.
functions.lesson.8: Normally a function gets a **copy** of each value. If it changes the copy, the caller's variable stays the same. With `ref` before the parameter, the function works on the caller's variable itself.
functions.lesson.11: D has **UFCS** (Uniform Function Call Syntax): you can write `f(x)` as `x.f()`, and `f(x, y)` as `x.f(y)`. When there is nothing left in the parentheses, you can drop them: `x.f`. This is why `s.toUpper()` from the strings unit works. Chains read from left to right.
functions.lesson.13: Use UFCS when it makes the order of steps easier to read: `3.plus(2).square` first adds, then squares.
functions.card.0: `int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }`
functions.card.2: `int f(int x, int y = 10)` has a default value
functions.card.3: `ref int n` changes the caller's variable
functions.card.4: UFCS: `f(x, y)` is the same as `x.f(y)`
functions-1.explain: The inner call gives `6`, and the outer call doubles it to `12`.
functions-2.explain: With `ref`, `a` is the variable `v` itself, so `v` becomes `10`.
functions-3.explain: With UFCS, `10.sub(4)` is the same as `sub(10, 4)`, which is `6`.
functions-4.explain: Without `ref`, `bump` changes only its own copy. `x` in `main` stays `3`.
functions-5.prompt: Which call means the same as `add(5, 2)`?
functions-5.explain: With UFCS the first argument goes before the dot: `add(5, 2)` becomes `5.add(2)`.
functions-6.explain: When `n` is not greater than 0, the function reaches its end without `return`. D stops with an error.
functions-7.prompt: Complete the function so that the program prints `9`.
functions-7.explain: `return` gives the value back to the caller, and `main` prints it.
functions-8.prompt: Complete the parameter so that the program prints `6`.
functions-8.explain: Only with `ref` does the function change `x` itself. `const` and `immutable` parameters cannot be changed at all.
functions-9.prompt: Build the first line of a function `isAdult` that takes an `int` called `age` and gives back a `bool`.
functions-9.explain: The return type comes first, then the name and the parameter with its type. A `void` function could not return a `bool`.
functions-10.prompt: Put the lines in order so that `larger` gives back the larger of two numbers.
functions-10.explain: If `a` is greater, the function returns `a`. Otherwise it reaches the last `return` and gives back `b`.
functions-11.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
arrays.title: Arrays
arrays.summary: Keep many values in dynamic arrays, append with ~=, cut slices and look up values by key in associative arrays.
arrays.lesson.0: An **array** holds several values of the same type in a fixed order. `int[]` is an array of `int` values. You write the values in square brackets. `a[0]` is the first element, `a.length` the number of elements, and `writeln` can print the whole array.
arrays.lesson.2: These arrays are **dynamic**: they can grow. `~=` adds an element (or another array) at the end, and `~` joins two arrays into a new one.
arrays.lesson.4: `foreach` walks over all elements. With two names, like `foreach (i, name; names)`, you also get the position.
arrays.lesson.7: `a[1 .. 4]` is a slice, as with strings, and `$` is the length. A slice does not copy the elements: it **shares** them with the array, so a change through the slice changes the array too. The same is true for `b = a`. `.dup` makes a real copy.
arrays.lesson.9: An index outside the array, like `nums[5]` for an array with 5 elements, stops the program with an error. The last valid index is `nums.length - 1`.
arrays.lesson.11: An **associative array** stores values under keys. `int[string] ages` has `string` keys and `int` values: the value type comes first, the key type goes in the brackets. `ages["Ana"] = 30` adds or changes a value. `"Ben" in ages` checks if a key exists, and `remove` deletes one.
arrays.lesson.13: Reading a key that does not exist stops the program with an error. `ages.get("Zoe", 0)` gives `0` instead. The order of the keys is not fixed, so do not rely on it.
arrays-1.explain: `a[1]` is `8` and `a[$ - 1]` is the last element, `16`. 8 + 16 is 24.
arrays-2.explain: Two elements are added to the two at the start: `[1, 2, 3, 1]` has 4 elements.
arrays-3.explain: The slice takes positions 2 and 3, which hold `7` and `8`. Position 4 is not included.
arrays-4.explain: `b = a` does not copy the elements. Both names share them, so the change through `b` is visible in `a`.
arrays-5.options.0: The program stops with an error.
arrays-5.explain: The array has the indexes 0, 1 and 2. Index 3 is outside, so the program stops with an error.
arrays-6.explain: `~=` with an array adds all of its elements. `fruits` has 4 elements: fig, kiwi, lime and date.
arrays-7.prompt: Complete the code so that it prints `[1, 2, 3]`.
arrays-7.explain: `~=` adds an element at the end. `~` alone creates a new array but does not store it.
arrays-8.prompt: Complete the code so that it prints `found`.
arrays-8.explain: `key in array` checks if an associative array has the key.
arrays-9.prompt: Build a line that creates an array `colors` with the strings "red" and "blue".
arrays-9.explain: An array of strings has the type `string[]`, and its values go in square brackets.
arrays-10.prompt: Put the lines in order so that the program prints `[3, 4]`.
arrays-10.explain: After both appends `a` is `[1, 2, 3, 4]`, and the slice from position 2 to the end is `[3, 4]`.
arrays-11.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
arrays-12.explain: There are 3 names with the indexes 0 to 2. The last one is `names[2]` (or `names[$ - 1]`).
structs.title: Structs and classes
structs.summary: Build your own types: structs with fields and methods, and classes with constructors, new and inheritance.
structs.lesson.0: A `struct` groups related values under one name and so creates a new type. The values inside are called **fields**. `Point(3, 4)` creates a `Point` and fills the fields in order. You reach a field with a dot: `p.x`.
structs.lesson.2: A function inside a struct is called a **method**. It can use the fields directly. You call it with a dot, like `r.area()`. As with UFCS, you can leave out empty parentheses.
structs.lesson.4: Structs are **values**: `b = a` copies all fields, so changing `b` leaves `a` as it was. A field can have a default value, like `int count = 0;`.
structs.lesson.7: A `class` also has fields and methods, but you create objects with `new`. A class variable is a **reference**: after `b = a`, both names point to the same object. The method `this(...)` is the **constructor**; `new` calls it. Inside, `this.owner` means the field, while `owner` alone is the parameter.
structs.lesson.9: A class can build on another class: `class Dog : Animal` gets all fields and methods of `Animal`. `super(name)` calls the constructor of `Animal`, and `override` replaces a method. A `Dog` object can be stored in an `Animal` variable and still uses its own method.
structs.lesson.11: A class variable without `new` is `null`: it points to no object. Calling a method on it crashes the program.
structs.lesson.12: Use a `struct` for small values like points or dates. Use a `class` when several parts of the program must share one object, or when you need inheritance.
structs.card.0: `struct P { int x; int y; }` and `P(1, 2)`
structs.card.1: methods are functions inside a struct or class
structs.card.2: structs are copied, class objects are shared
structs-2.explain: A struct is copied on assignment. Changing `q` does not change `p`.
structs-3.explain: `c` and `d` point to the same object, so the change through `d` is visible through `c`.
structs-4.explain: `writeln` prints a struct as its name followed by the field values in parentheses.
structs-5.explain: The method uses the field `c`: 100 * 9 / 5 + 32 is 212.
structs-6.explain: Objects of a class are created with `new`: `Car c = new Car();`.
structs-7.prompt: Complete the constructor so that the program prints `Lea`.
structs-7.explain: In D the constructor is always called `this`, whatever the name of the class.
structs-8.prompt: Complete the code so that `Cat` builds on `Animal` and the program prints `Meow`.
structs-8.explain: D uses a colon for inheritance: `class Cat : Animal`. `extends` is Java.
structs-9.prompt: Build a line that creates a new `Account` for "Ana" with the balance 100 and stores it in the variable `acc`.
structs-9.explain: `new` creates the object and calls the constructor with the two arguments.
structs-10.prompt: Put the lines in order so that the program prints `1 5`.
structs-10.explain: `q` is a copy of `p`. Only the copy gets the new `x`, so `p.x` stays `1`.
structs-11.prompt: Match the code with its meaning.
structs-11.pairs.3: replaces a method of the parent class
structs-12.explain: `lamp` is `null` because no object was created. Write `Lamp lamp = new Lamp();`.
